questions.stem: An atom of chlorine-37 has an atomic number of 17. How many neutrons are in its nucleus?
questions.explanation: The mass number, 37, is the number of protons plus neutrons, and the atomic number, 17, is the number of protons, so there are 37 − 17 = 20 neutrons. 17 is the number of protons (and electrons in the neutral atom), not neutrons.

questions.stem: A particle has 16 protons, 16 neutrons and 18 electrons. Which particle is it?
options: An argon atom, Ar, with a mass number of 34
A sulfur atom, S, with mass number 34
A sulfur ion, S2+, with mass number 32
A sulfide ion, S2−, with mass number 32
questions.explanation: Sixteen protons makes it sulfur, and 16 + 16 gives a mass number of 32. Two more electrons than protons gives a charge of 2−, so it is the sulfide ion. Argon has 18 protons, so having 18 electrons does not make a particle argon.

questions.stem: What is the subshell electronic configuration of a potassium atom?
options: 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶ 4s¹
1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶ 3d¹
1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁵ 4s²
1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁴ 3d³
questions.explanation: Potassium has 19 electrons. After 3p is full, the 4s subshell is lower in energy than 3d, so the 19th electron goes into 4s. A 3p subshell holds six electrons and fills completely before 4s begins.

questions.stem: An element has the electronic configuration 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁴. Where is it in the periodic table?
options: Group 4, period 3
Group 14, period 3
Group 16, period 4
Group 16, period 3
questions.explanation: The outer shell is the third, so the element is in period 3. It has six valence electrons in 3s and 3p, which places it in group 16: it is sulfur. Group 4 comes from counting only the four 3p electrons and ignoring the two 3s electrons.

questions.stem: Which trend is seen across period 3 from sodium to argon?
options: Atomic radius decreases and first ionisation energy generally increases
Atomic radius increases and first ionisation energy generally decreases
Atomic radius decreases and first ionisation energy generally decreases
Atomic radius increases and first ionisation energy generally increases
questions.explanation: Core charge rises across the period while the valence electrons stay in the third shell, so they are pulled closer and held more tightly. Smaller atoms with more strongly held electrons need more energy to remove the first electron. A larger number of electrons does not make atoms bigger here, because no new shell is added.

questions.stem: Atomic radius decreases across period 3 even though each element has one more electron than the one before. What is the best explanation?
options: Each element adds a new electron shell that is held more tightly
The number of neutrons increases, which pulls the electron shells inward
Core charge increases while the valence electrons stay in the same shell
The extra electrons repel each other and are pushed closer to the nucleus
questions.explanation: Each step adds a proton to the nucleus and an electron to the same outer shell, so the core charge felt by the valence electrons rises from +1 to +8 and the shell is drawn in. Repulsion between electrons would push them apart, not closer. Neutrons carry no charge, so they do not attract electrons.

questions.stem: Why does reactivity increase down group 1 from lithium to caesium?
options: Each atom has more valence electrons to give away when it reacts
Electronegativity increases, so the atoms attract electrons more readily
The valence electron is further from the nucleus and is lost more easily
The core charge increases, so the valence electron is held more strongly
questions.explanation: Group 1 metals react by losing their single valence electron. Going down the group adds shells, so that electron is further from the nucleus and more shielded, and less energy is needed to remove it. The core charge stays at +1 down a group, and every group 1 atom has one valence electron.

questions.stem: Which change occurs going down group 17 from fluorine to iodine?
options: Electronegativity decreases and reactivity increases
Electronegativity increases and reactivity decreases
Atomic radius decreases and reactivity decreases
Electronegativity and reactivity both decrease
questions.explanation: Halogens react by gaining an electron. Down the group the atoms get larger, so an incoming electron is further from the nucleus and attracted less strongly, which lowers both electronegativity and reactivity. Reactivity rising down a group is the pattern for metals in group 1, not for non-metals.

questions.stem: Rare-earth elements such as neodymium are described as critical elements mainly because they:
options: are gases at room temperature that escape to the atmosphere when used
are essential to technologies such as wind turbine magnets and their supply is at risk
are radioactive, so they must be stored safely as soon as they are mined
are the most abundant metals in Earth's crust but are costly to purify
questions.explanation: An element is critical when modern technology depends on it and its supply could be disrupted. Neodymium magnets are used in wind turbines and electric vehicle motors, while economic deposits are few and concentrated in a small number of countries. Neodymium is a solid metal and is not one of the most abundant elements in the crust.

questions.stem: Helium is considered a critical element even though it is not used up in chemical reactions. Which reason best explains this?
options: It reacts with oxygen in the air, so a sample can be used only once
It is radioactive and decays into hydrogen while it is in storage
It forms stable compounds in landfill that cannot be broken down
Once released, it escapes Earth's atmosphere and is very hard to recover
questions.explanation: Helium is unreactive, but it is so light that once released it rises and escapes to space. Supplies come mainly from natural gas deposits, so recovering and recycling it, for example from MRI machines, is important. As a noble gas it does not react with oxygen or form compounds.

questions.stem: How many lone (non-bonding) pairs of electrons are on the nitrogen atom in the Lewis structure of ammonia, NH₃?
options: Three
Four
One
Two
questions.explanation: Nitrogen has five valence electrons. Three are used in the three N–H single bonds, which leaves two electrons, or one lone pair. Three is the number of bonding pairs, not lone pairs.

questions.stem: Which description matches the Lewis structure of a nitrogen molecule, N₂?
options: A triple bond, with one lone pair on each nitrogen atom
A double bond, with two lone pairs on each nitrogen atom
A single bond, with three lone pairs on each nitrogen atom
A triple bond, with no lone pairs on either nitrogen atom
questions.explanation: Each nitrogen has five valence electrons and needs three more to reach eight, so the atoms share three pairs in a triple bond. The remaining two electrons on each atom form one lone pair. A double bond with two lone pairs on each atom describes an oxygen molecule.

questions.stem: According to VSEPR theory, what is the shape of a water molecule?
options: Pyramidal
Tetrahedral
Bent
Linear
questions.explanation: Oxygen has four electron pairs around it, two bonding and two lone pairs, which repel each other into a tetrahedral arrangement. The shape is named from the atoms only, so with two hydrogen atoms it is bent. It is not linear, because the lone pairs push the bonds together.

questions.stem: Why is an ammonia molecule pyramidal rather than flat?
options: The three hydrogen atoms attract one another and pull towards one side
Nitrogen forms a double bond to one of the hydrogen atoms, bending the shape
The polar N–H bonds make the hydrogen atoms repel the nitrogen atom
The lone pair on nitrogen repels the three bonding pairs, giving four electron groups
questions.explanation: Nitrogen has three bonding pairs and one lone pair, and these four electron groups repel to point towards the corners of a tetrahedron. With atoms at only three corners, the shape is pyramidal. Hydrogen can form only one bond, so a double bond to hydrogen is impossible.

questions.stem: Carbon dioxide contains polar C=O bonds but is a non-polar molecule. Why?
options: Its double bonds share the electrons equally between carbon and oxygen
Its linear shape is symmetrical, so the two bond dipoles cancel
Carbon and oxygen have equal electronegativities, so the bonds are non-polar
Its bent shape places both oxygen atoms on the same side of the carbon
questions.explanation: Oxygen is more electronegative than carbon, so each C=O bond is polar. Because the molecule is linear, the two equal dipoles point in opposite directions and cancel, leaving no overall dipole. The molecule is not bent, and the bonds themselves are not shared equally.

questions.stem: Tetrachloromethane, CCl₄, and trichloromethane, CHCl₃, both have a tetrahedral shape. Which statement is correct?
options: Both are non-polar because a tetrahedral shape always cancels bond dipoles
CCl₄ is polar because it contains more polar bonds than CHCl₃ does
CHCl₃ is polar because its bond dipoles do not cancel, while CCl₄ is non-polar
Both are polar because each molecule contains polar C–Cl bonds
questions.explanation: In CCl₄ four identical C–Cl dipoles point symmetrically to the corners of a tetrahedron and cancel. In CHCl₃ one corner is a less polar C–H bond, so the dipoles no longer balance and the molecule is polar. Having polar bonds is not enough: polarity depends on whether the shape lets the dipoles cancel.

questions.stem: Which of these is the strongest?
options: A dipole-dipole attraction between HCl molecules
Dispersion forces between methane molecules
An O–H covalent bond in a water molecule
A hydrogen bond between water molecules
questions.explanation: Covalent bonds within molecules are much stronger than any intermolecular force. Hydrogen bonds are the strongest intermolecular forces, but they are still only a small fraction of the strength of an O–H covalent bond.

questions.stem: When liquid water boils, what is overcome?
options: Covalent bonds between the oxygen and hydrogen atoms in each molecule
Ionic bonds between H+ and OH− ions held in the liquid
Hydrogen bonds between the oxygen and hydrogen atoms in each molecule
Hydrogen bonds and dispersion forces between the water molecules
questions.explanation: Boiling separates whole molecules from each other, so only the intermolecular forces are overcome; the steam is still H₂O. The O–H bonds inside each molecule are covalent and stay intact. A hydrogen bond is an attraction between molecules, not the bond within one.

questions.stem: Between molecules of which substance does hydrogen bonding occur?
options: Ammonia, NH₃
Methane, CH₄
Hydrogen chloride, HCl
Hydrogen, H₂
questions.explanation: Hydrogen bonding needs a hydrogen atom bonded to nitrogen, oxygen or fluorine, which leaves it strongly positive and able to attract a lone pair on a neighbouring molecule. Ammonia has N–H bonds. In HCl the hydrogen is bonded to chlorine rather than to N, O or F, so its molecules are held by dipole-dipole attraction instead.

questions.stem: Methane (CH₄, molar mass 16 g mol⁻¹) boils at −162 °C, while ammonia (NH₃, 17 g mol⁻¹) boils at −33 °C. What best explains the difference?
options: Ammonia molecules are held by hydrogen bonds, which are stronger than the forces between methane molecules
Ammonia has a higher molar mass, so its dispersion forces are much stronger than methane's
N–H bonds are stronger than C–H bonds, so more energy is needed to break ammonia apart
Methane molecules are polar and repel each other, which lowers its boiling point
questions.explanation: The two molecules have almost the same molar mass and number of electrons, so their dispersion forces are similar. Ammonia also forms hydrogen bonds through its N–H bonds, and extra energy is needed to overcome them. Boiling does not break covalent bonds, so the strength of N–H compared with C–H bonds is irrelevant.

questions.stem: Why do molecular substances not conduct electricity in either the solid or the liquid state?
options: Their ions are held in fixed positions by strong covalent bonds
They are made of neutral molecules, with no charged particles free to move
Their covalent bonds hold the electrons too far away from the nuclei
Their molecules are too large to move between the electrodes
questions.explanation: Conduction needs mobile charged particles, either ions or delocalised electrons. In a molecular substance every electron is held in a bond or lone pair within a neutral molecule, so melting frees molecules but not charges. Molecular substances contain no ions to be fixed or freed.

questions.stem: The boiling points of the halogens increase from fluorine to iodine. Why?
options: The molecules become more polar as the atoms get larger
Larger molecules with more electrons have stronger dispersion forces
The covalent bond in each molecule gets stronger down the group
Hydrogen bonding between the molecules gets stronger down the group
questions.explanation: Halogen molecules are non-polar, so dispersion forces are the only forces between them. Larger molecules with more electrons form bigger temporary dipoles, so the dispersion forces strengthen and more energy is needed to boil. There is no hydrogen in a halogen molecule, so hydrogen bonding is impossible.

questions.stem: Why does graphite conduct electricity?
options: Its layers are held together by ionic bonds that release ions when a voltage is applied
Each carbon forms four bonds, and these bonding electrons can jump between the atoms
The weak forces between its layers allow whole layers to carry the charge
Each carbon forms three bonds, leaving one delocalised electron that moves along the layers
questions.explanation: In graphite each carbon is covalently bonded to three others in a flat layer. The fourth valence electron of each atom is delocalised across the layer and can move when a voltage is applied. Graphite contains no ions, and in diamond, where all four electrons are in bonds, there is no conduction.

questions.stem: Diamond is used in drill bits for cutting rock. Which feature of its structure explains this use?
options: Strong dispersion forces hold its separate carbon molecules tightly together
Each carbon is covalently bonded to four others in a rigid three-dimensional network
Its layers of carbon atoms slide easily over one another as it cuts the rock
Its delocalised electrons make it hard and a good conductor of electricity
questions.explanation: Diamond is a covalent network lattice: every carbon is bonded to four others in all directions, so scratching or breaking it means breaking many strong covalent bonds. Sliding layers describe graphite, which is soft. Diamond has no delocalised electrons and does not conduct electricity.

questions.stem: Diamond and graphite both have very high melting points, but only graphite is soft enough to be used as a lubricant. Which explains this difference?
options: Graphite has much weaker covalent bonds within its layers than diamond has between its atoms
Diamond contains carbon ions in a lattice while graphite contains neutral carbon atoms
Graphite has delocalised electrons that act as a lubricant between its individual atoms
Graphite's layers are held by weak dispersion forces, while diamond's bonds are covalent in every direction
questions.explanation: Melting either form means breaking strong covalent bonds, which is why both melt at very high temperatures. In graphite, though, the layers are attracted to each other only by weak dispersion forces, so they slide apart easily. The covalent bonds within graphite's layers are at least as strong as diamond's, so weaker bonds do not explain the softness.

questions.stem: Which model best describes metallic bonding?
options: Positive and negative ions held together in a fixed, rigid lattice
Atoms sharing pairs of electrons in strong directional bonds
Neutral atoms held together by weak dispersion forces
A lattice of cations surrounded by a sea of delocalised electrons
questions.explanation: Metal atoms release their valence electrons, which become delocalised throughout the lattice of positive ions, and the electrostatic attraction between cations and electrons is the metallic bond. A lattice of positive and negative ions describes an ionic compound, and shared electron pairs describe covalent bonding.

questions.stem: Metals are malleable because:
options: ions of like charge move next to each other and repel when force is applied
the cations can slide past each other while staying attracted to the delocalised electrons
the metal atoms are held together only by weak dispersion forces
the covalent bonds between metal atoms can bend without breaking
questions.explanation: Metallic bonding is non-directional: the sea of delocalised electrons moves with the cations, so layers can shift without the attraction being lost and the metal changes shape instead of shattering. Like charges meeting and repelling is why ionic crystals are brittle. Metals are not held by covalent bonds or by dispersion forces.

questions.stem: Three metals were tested. X reacted vigorously with cold water. Y did not react with cold water but bubbled in dilute hydrochloric acid. Z reacted with neither. What is the order of reactivity, most reactive first?
options: Z, Y, X
Y, X, Z
X, Z, Y
X, Y, Z
questions.explanation: Reacting with cold water shows X is very easily oxidised, so it is most reactive. Y is oxidised by acid but not by water, so it is less reactive than X, and Z, which is not oxidised by either, is least reactive. Putting Z first reverses the series.

questions.stem: In a reactivity series based on reactions with water, acids and oxygen, metals near the top of the series are those that:
options: gain electrons most readily, so they are most easily reduced
share electrons most readily, so they form covalent oxides
lose protons most readily, so they form positive ions fastest
lose electrons most readily, so they are most easily oxidised
questions.explanation: Each of these reactions oxidises the metal to its positive ion, so the more readily a metal loses electrons the more vigorously it reacts. Gaining electrons is reduction, which is what happens to the water, acid or oxygen. Metals never lose protons when they react.

questions.stem: Which description best fits a circular economy for aluminium cans?
options: Used cans are incinerated to recover energy from the metal
Cans are made thicker so that each one lasts longer before landfill
Used cans are collected and remelted to make new cans
Bauxite is mined, refined and made into cans that go to landfill
questions.explanation: In a circular economy materials are kept in use: aluminium from used cans is reprocessed into the same product again. Mining, using and then landfilling the metal is the take–make–dispose pattern of a linear economy. Making cans thicker still ends in landfill.

questions.stem: Producing aluminium by recycling is more sustainable than extracting it from bauxite mainly because recycling:
options: converts the aluminium into a more useful element during remelting
always produces purer aluminium than metal made from new ore
removes the need to use any energy, because the metal is already pure
needs far less energy than extracting the metal from its ore
questions.explanation: Extracting aluminium from its ore by electrolysis uses a great deal of electricity, whereas remelting scrap aluminium needs only a small fraction of that energy and avoids new mining. Remelting still uses energy, and recycling cannot change aluminium into another element.

questions.stem: Sodium chloride conducts electricity when molten but not when solid. Why?
options: When solid its covalent bonds hold all the electrons in place
When solid it contains no ions, only neutral atoms
When molten its ions are free to move and carry charge
When molten it releases delocalised electrons that carry charge
questions.explanation: Solid sodium chloride contains Na+ and Cl− ions held in fixed positions in the lattice. Melting frees the ions to move towards the electrodes, which is the current. Ionic compounds have no delocalised electrons, which are a feature of metals.

questions.stem: Ionic crystals are brittle because a sharp blow:
options: shifts a layer so that ions of like charge line up and repel
breaks the covalent bonds between neighbouring ions
removes the delocalised electrons that hold the ions together
separates molecules that are held by weak intermolecular forces
questions.explanation: In an ionic lattice each ion is surrounded by ions of opposite charge. A force that moves one layer brings like charges next to each other, and their repulsion splits the crystal. Ions are held by ionic, not covalent, bonds, and there are no delocalised electrons or molecules in an ionic lattice.

questions.stem: What is the formula of ammonium phosphate?
options: (NH₄)₂PO₄
(NH₄)₃PO₄
NH₄PO₄
NH₄(PO₄)₃
questions.explanation: The ammonium ion is NH₄+ and the phosphate ion is PO₄3−, so three ammonium ions balance one phosphate ion. Brackets show that the whole NH₄ group is taken three times. NH₄PO₄ would leave a charge of 2−.

questions.stem: What is the formula of iron(III) sulfate?
options: Fe₂(SO₄)₃
FeSO₄
Fe₃(SO₄)₂
Fe(SO₄)₃
questions.explanation: The Roman numeral shows the ion is Fe3+, and sulfate is SO₄2−. The lowest whole-number ratio that balances +3 and −2 is two Fe3+ (+6) to three SO₄2− (−6). FeSO₄ is iron(II) sulfate, made from Fe2+.

questions.stem: What is the name of the compound Ca(HCO₃)₂?
options: Calcium carbonate
Calcium hydroxide carbonate
Calcium dihydrogen carbonate
Calcium hydrogen carbonate
questions.explanation: HCO₃− is the hydrogen carbonate ion, and two are needed to balance one Ca2+ ion. The subscript 2 outside the bracket is not part of the ion's name. Calcium carbonate is CaCO₃, which contains the CO₃2− ion.

questions.stem: When magnesium burns in oxygen to form magnesium oxide, what happens to the electrons?
options: Each oxygen atom transfers two electrons to a magnesium atom
Magnesium and oxygen atoms share two pairs of electrons
Each magnesium atom transfers only one electron to an oxygen atom
Each magnesium atom transfers two electrons to an oxygen atom
questions.explanation: Magnesium, a metal in group 2, loses its two valence electrons to form Mg2+, and oxygen gains them to form O2−, giving MgO. Metals lose electrons rather than gain them. Transferring only one electron would give Mg+ and O−, which are not the stable ions.

questions.stem: Silver nitrate solution is added to sodium chloride solution and a white precipitate forms. Which is the correct ionic equation?
options: Ag+(aq) + Cl−(aq) → AgCl(aq)
AgNO₃(aq) + NaCl(aq) → AgCl(aq) + NaNO₃(s)
Ag+(aq) + Cl−(aq) → AgCl(s)
Na+(aq) + NO₃−(aq) → NaNO₃(s)
questions.explanation: Silver chloride is insoluble, so it is the white solid, AgCl(s). Sodium and nitrate ions stay dissolved as spectator ions and are left out of the ionic equation. Writing AgCl as (aq) would mean no precipitate had formed.

questions.stem: Barium nitrate solution is mixed with sodium sulfate solution. Barium sulfate is insoluble in water. Which ions are spectator ions?
options: Ba2+ and Na+
SO₄2− and NO₃−
Na+ and NO₃−
Ba2+ and SO₄2−
questions.explanation: Ba2+ and SO₄2− combine to form the precipitate, BaSO₄(s), so they take part in the reaction. Na+ and NO₃− remain dissolved in the solution before and after mixing, so they are spectators. The ionic equation is Ba2+(aq) + SO₄2−(aq) → BaSO₄(s).

questions.stem: An unknown solution contains one of Ag+, Ba2+, Na+ or NH₄+. Adding sodium chloride solution gives no precipitate, but adding sodium sulfate solution gives a white precipitate. Which cation is present?
options: Na+
NH₄+
Ba2+
Ag+
questions.explanation: Silver ions would form an insoluble chloride, so the lack of a precipitate with chloride rules out Ag+. Sodium and ammonium compounds are all soluble, so neither would precipitate with sulfate. Barium chloride is soluble but barium sulfate is not, which matches both results.

questions.stem: Which substance is most likely to dissolve in hexane, a non-polar solvent?
options: Sodium chloride, NaCl
Copper(II) sulfate, CuSO₄
Glucose, C₆H₁₂O₆
Iodine, I₂
questions.explanation: Like dissolves like: non-polar iodine molecules mix with non-polar hexane molecules through dispersion forces. Ionic compounds such as sodium chloride and copper(II) sulfate, and polar glucose with its many O–H groups, dissolve in polar water instead.

questions.stem: Why does ammonia dissolve readily in water?
options: Ammonia reacts completely with water to form ammonium chloride
Water breaks the N–H covalent bonds and releases hydrogen ions
Ammonia and water molecules form hydrogen bonds with each other
Ammonia molecules are non-polar and fit between the water molecules
questions.explanation: Ammonia is polar and has N–H bonds and a lone pair, so its molecules form hydrogen bonds with water molecules, which is why it is very soluble. Ammonia is polar, not non-polar. No chloride is present, so ammonium chloride cannot form.

questions.stem: In paper chromatography the solvent front travelled 8.0 cm from the origin and a dye spot travelled 3.2 cm. What is the Rf value of the dye?
questions.explanation: Rf = distance moved by the component ÷ distance moved by the solvent front = 3.2 ÷ 8.0 = 0.40. An Rf value can never be more than 1, so 2.5, which divides the wrong way, cannot be right. 0.60 uses the distance between the spot and the front instead.

questions.stem: A component has an Rf value of 0.65. In a chromatogram where the solvent front is 6.0 cm from the origin, how far from the origin will its spot be?
options: 3.9 cm
9.2 cm
2.1 cm
5.4 cm
questions.explanation: Rearranging Rf = component distance ÷ solvent distance gives component distance = 0.65 × 6.0 = 3.9 cm. 9.2 cm comes from dividing 6.0 by 0.65, which would place the spot beyond the solvent front. 2.1 cm uses 0.35 instead of 0.65.

questions.stem: In thin-layer chromatography with a polar stationary phase and a non-polar solvent, component A has a smaller Rf value than component B. Which conclusion is best supported?
options: A is more polar than B, so it adsorbs more strongly to the stationary phase
A is less polar than B, so it dissolves more readily in the mobile phase
A has a larger molar mass than B, so it is heavier and moves more slowly
A is present in a smaller amount than B, so its spot has moved a shorter distance
questions.explanation: A component that is attracted more strongly to the polar stationary phase spends less time in the moving solvent and travels a shorter distance. A more polar A fits this. A component that dissolved more in the mobile phase would travel further, and the amount of a component does not change its Rf value.
